articles.title: Factry Historian vs InfluxDB: buy a historian or build one on a time-series database
articles.excerpt: This isn't a classic head-to-head. Factry Historian actually stores its time series in InfluxDB (v1.x and v2.x are the supported back ends), with configuration, metadata and events in PostgreSQL. So t…
articles.body: This isn't a classic head-to-head. Factry Historian actually stores its time series in InfluxDB (v1.x and v2.x are the supported back ends), with configuration, metadata and events in PostgreSQL. So the real question is whether you buy a finished process historian or build your own around a general-purpose time-series database. What you get Factry Historian is a complete process historian: collectors, asset models, event processing and a Grafana plugin, sold as one product. InfluxDB is a database for event and time-series data. Collection, modeling and dashboards are pieces you add yourself, for example with InfluxData's Telegraf agent.
articles.author: PlantWired

articles.title: My SQL JOIN Ran Perfectly and Doubled the Refunds
articles.excerpt: The SQL query ran without errors. The columns looked right. The totals seemed reasonable. Except Ava's refund total was $60. She'd only been refunded $30. No missing data. No syntax error. Nothing obv…
articles.body: The SQL query ran without errors. The columns looked right. The totals seemed reasonable. Except Ava's refund total was $60. She'd only been refunded $30. No missing data. No syntax error. Nothing obviously wrong with the query. SQL had done exactly what the query asked it to do. The problem was that the query wasn't asking the right question. Here's the idea that explains it: A JOIN doesn't guarantee one result row per row in your first table. One row can match multiple rows, and those matches can multiply your results. That might sound harmless until you start calculating totals. Let's reproduce the problem with a dataset small enough to check every number ourselves. Step 1: Four customers, six orders, three refunds Imagine we're building a report for an online store.
articles.author: Krishna

articles.title: Your Post Now Has to Be Nameable
articles.excerpt: For twenty years, creators fed the algorithm indirectly — watch time, shares, dwell — and hoped it inferred the rest. That era just ended. Instagram, Facebook, Threads, YouTube, and TikTok have all gi…
articles.body: For twenty years, creators fed the algorithm indirectly — watch time, shares, dwell — and hoped it inferred the rest. That era just ended. Instagram, Facebook, Threads, YouTube, and TikTok have all given users a text box: type what you want more of, in your own words. The algorithm now takes requests. And a request can only match a post whose topic can be named — in the audience's language, not yours. My own grid taught me this the expensive way: posts I could describe only in jargon sat at 17 to 49 views, while a personal story a stranger could name in five words pulled 393. Here is the timeline nobody on the supply side seems to have priced in. TikTok's Manage Topics arrived in June 2025 — sliders, crude, but a precedent.
articles.author: Jiahui Miao

articles.title: Tailscale SSH checked paths as you and dialed them as root. I read all four bulletins.
articles.excerpt: Last weekend a security researcher published a report titled "Tailworm," describing vulnerabilities in Tailscale SSH and Tailscale Serve. This morning (October 28) Tailscale published its findings pos…
articles.body: Last weekend a security researcher published a report titled "Tailworm," describing vulnerabilities in Tailscale SSH and Tailscale Serve. This morning (October 28) Tailscale published its findings post and four security bulletins, TS-2026-014 through TS-2026-017, with fixes in v1.104.4 . I read all four bulletins. They describe four different bugs, but three of them are the same bug wearing different clothes: tailscaled runs as root, it checked permissions as if it were you, and then it acted as root. The timeline, because it matters Friday, October 23 — concerns about Tailscale SSH start circulating on social media; Tailscale begins investigating with external specialists. Saturday, October 24, morning — the researcher sends Tailscale the report, and publishes it two hours later.

Organizations also need a practical way to handle technical questions, resolve recurring problems, and help staff continue their work when something goes wrong. A reliable technical support system helps an organization respond consistently instead of depending on one person who happens to know how everything works.

articles.title: Astronomers found a mysterious object beyond Neptune, and it could be a new dwarf planet
articles.excerpt: The Vera Rubin Observatory has discovered a suspected dwarf planet beyond Neptune's orbit. If confirmed, it would be the sixth known dwarf planet in our solar system.
articles.body: The powerful Vera Rubin Observatory has spotted what seems to be a dwarf planet circling the sun in the frigid depths beyond Neptune. The icy object, known as 2026 ED138, is likely between 600 and 1500 kilometers (373 to 972 miles) wide, scientists say. It's therefore probably big enough to be sculpted into a sphere by its own gravity — a key characteristic that separates dwarf planets from asteroids and other small space rocks. And if 2026 ED138 is indeed a dwarf planet, that's a pretty big deal, as astronomers have confirmed just five of them to date: Pluto , Ceres, Eris, Haumea and Makemake . articles.title: Black holes can split in two — but only if they spin at extreme speeds
articles.excerpt: Scientists have long known that when two black holes collide, they merge to create a more massive black hole. New research suggests that the opposite may happen too: single black holes may split in tw…
articles.body: Scientists have long known that when two black holes collide, they merge to create a more massive black hole. These events are so violent that they set the very fabric of space ringing with ripples called gravitational waves. Now, new research suggests that the opposite may happen, too: single black holes may be able to split in two. But this can only happen if that progenitor black hole is spinning at maximum possible speed. That speed prevents the black holes from immediately falling back on each other. There are physical laws in place that would usually prevent black holes from splitting in two; the team behind this research investigated whether there are conditions in which these laws can be temporarily bypassed.
